title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
gist: Venture-backed sales-intelligence startups (Starbridge, Pursuit, PinPoint, NationGraph) and ChatGPT-drafted requests are flooding US federal, state and local public-records offices, turning FOIA into a monetized data feed for selling to government. Understaffed agencies are responding with AI-assisted processing and new state laws (California, Indiana, a pending Pennsylvania bill) that make it easier to deny requests, risking less transparency for everyone.

themes.theme: Public records as a sales-data business

insights.claim: Venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million over the last few years to collect public records from thousands of government agencies and turn them into AI-powered 'signals' that help businesses sell to governments.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: GovTech sales-intelligence is a funded category built on a free, publicly mandated input; watch for regulatory risk to that input.
insights.quote: venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments
insights.locator: Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US

insights.claim: Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (David Sacks's firm), to build a 'Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data' that matches agencies with vendors.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Signals investor appetite for proprietary public-sector data terminals; a comparable to track in GovTech funding.
insights.quote: Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data

insights.claim: Pursuit, backed by Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to identify likely government buyers using board minutes, budgets and what it calls 'an industrial-scale FOIA operation.'
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Pursuit's moat depends on high-volume FOIA harvesting, which is exactly what new state laws target.
insights.locator: Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley

insights.claim: SmartProcure (doing business as GovSpend) pioneered the standardized government-purchasing-data model about 15 years ago and relies on account teams with long-standing agency relationships, while newer AI startups flood agencies with requests to backfill historical data.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Incumbent relationship-based collection may prove more durable than startup volume-based scraping as agencies push back.

insights.claim: Request volumes from sales-data firms are enormous: PinPoint Analytics sent up to 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset (now about 500), SmartProcure and Pursuit send roughly 180,000 per year, and NationGraph claims about 10,000 per day on behalf of clients.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: The scale of automated harvesting explains the agency backlash and makes these business models a target for fee or denial rules.

insights.claim: Sales-data firms typically write records requests from templates rather than AI; AI is used downstream to standardize returned spreadsheets, PDFs and mailed packets and turn them into branded sales signals and pricing benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: The AI value-add is in normalization of messy government data, which is the defensible part if records become proactively published.
insights.quote: The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI.

insights.claim: Commercial requesters have historically dominated FOIA, accounting for 79% to 96% of requests at federal agencies such as the EPA and FDA, per Margaret Kwoka's 2016 'FOIA, Inc.' study.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: FOIA has long been a commercial data pipe; AI accelerates an existing pattern rather than creating a new one.
insights.locator: This is why businesses, with the time and resources

insights.claim: Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million public records requests last year, attributed partly to AI, mass filings by the Heritage Foundation, and immigrants seeking their own records.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Rising FOIA load creates demand for records-management and redaction software at the federal level.

insights.claim: An AI-detector analysis of the US Department of Education's July request log found at least 29% of requests were written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025; AI-written requests were twice as long and 83% asked for long lists of records.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: AI-generated requests impose disproportionate per-request processing cost on agencies.
insights.locator: David Cuillier, director of the Brechner

insights.claim: Pennsylvania's Office of Open Records appeals rose from about 3,000 in 2021 to just under 4,000 in 2025 and are projected at 6,000 this year, a surge not tied to any hot-button issue but to AI-driven activity, with chatbots encouraging hopeless appeals and some filings containing hallucinated legal citations.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Chatbot-encouraged litigation-style filings are a measurable public-sector cost of consumer AI.

insights.claim: Local offices are being overwhelmed: Chautauqua County, NY hired a paralegal after requests doubled, and Ann Arbor's requests rose from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year, with FOIA consuming about half the chief deputy clerk's day.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Municipal headcount/budget pressure from AI request volume supports demand for request-portal software.

insights.claim: One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to search for records, and DHS is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates fear could entrench over-withholding.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: AI is entering both sides of FOIA, creating a software arms race between requesters and records offices.
insights.locator: On the other side of the records requests

insights.claim: CivicPlus's NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots, but cannot determine whether a human used AI to draft a request.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Local governments migrating from email to centralized portals is a GovTech adoption tailwind for vendors like CivicPlus.
insights.quote: doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request

insights.claim: More than 20 state and federal measures affecting public records are in play this year, several giving agencies new ways to deny requests; California's law signed in September declares AI systems are not 'members of the public', and a stalled Pennsylvania bill would allow denying requests reasonably suspected to be AI- or script-generated.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Regulatory tightening threatens the input pipeline of FOIA-dependent data startups.
insights.quote: at an ordinary human volume and frequency
insights.locator: As volumes rise, legislatures are responding

insights.claim: Indiana passed, without a single dissenting vote, a law effective July 1 that lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents and deny suspected data-scraping or phishing requests, after Allen County reported 'suspiciously non-human' requests eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Unanimous passage suggests bipartisan appetite to curb commercial records harvesting; expect copycat state laws.

insights.claim: Adams County, Indiana banned commercial use and resale of its records in March; requests fell from up to 10 a week back to one to five after the state law took effect, though the ban itself is hard to enforce.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Local resale bans are weakly enforceable, but combined with state law they measurably cut request volume.

insights.claim: The biggest risk of reforms aimed at bulk AI requests and sales-tech crawlers is collateral damage to out-of-state reporters, academic researchers and immigration lawyers, potentially making government less transparent.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Watch for transparency-advocate pushback that could shape how restrictive final rules become.

themes.theme: Who pays: fees and proactive disclosure

insights.claim: Agencies recoup less than 5% of their FOIA costs from commercial requesters despite a 1986 amendment allowing higher commercial fees; at the FDA in one studied year, fees were $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Commercial data firms effectively get a taxpayer-subsidized input; fee reform is a latent cost risk to their unit economics.
insights.quote: It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t

insights.claim: Proactive 'affirmative disclosure' of commonly requested data (e.g., EPA's online property contamination records, California's Open FI$Cal spending portal) could reduce request load, but such portals omit the full contracts sales-tech firms want, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses and service commitments.
insights.speaker: Matthew King
insights.so_what: Full-contract data is the scarce asset; startups claiming they'd survive free publication would then compete mainly on analytics.
insights.quote: The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there
